rubrics.criterion: No helper family's per-call record carries members of a cross-family capability protocol that the family never reads, writes, or overrides: after the repair, each record-producing or record-consuming helper family (downlevel generator record, sync iterator adapter, async generator, async delegator, async-values adapter, decorator application contexts, and the two disposal-environment helpers) exposes on its records only capabilities that family itself exercises or its callers supply.
rubrics.rationale: This case's central obligation is that the record surfaces stop being forced through one shared capability kit spanning unrelated helper families; the repo test layout runs every helper in all three emission formats, so any leftover forced member is observable per family.

rubrics.criterion: Every helper signature that was routed through the shared record protocol in the declaration file is annotated with a type that describes that helper's own record or input shape (a helper-specific interface, its original concrete annotation, or an equivalent narrow type), rather than one protocol shared across unrelated helper signatures.
rubrics.rationale: The declaration file is the published boundary every downstream type-check resolves; routing one interface through the generator, iterator, decorator, and disposal signatures was the declaration-side half of this case.

rubrics.criterion: The behavior-carrying logic that the shared kit took over for three families is served by family-internal implementations again: decorator-result validation and the addInitializer enqueue in the decorator helper, the return-path promise wiring in the async generator, and the step settlement in the async-values adapter each resolve through code owned by that family (a local helper, closure, or family-local equivalent) rather than through members installed by a cross-family protocol.
rubrics.rationale: In this instance three families do not merely carry unused surface: their glue was rewritten to read kit-provided members, so removing the kit without restoring family-local glue changes behavior at those exact call paths.

rubrics.criterion: The resolution is applied consistently to all three shipped runtime copies (the classic/UMD copy, the CommonJS copy, and the pure-ESM copy), so all three keep exporting the same names and any examination of one copy matches the corresponding helper in the others.
rubrics.rationale: The runtime is shipped as three separately consumed, behaviorally interchangeable copies of the same helper bodies; fixing one consumption mode and leaving others on the shared protocol is a half-finished repair specific to this repository's packaging.

rubrics.criterion: The runtime resolution and the declaration resolution land together: no declaration annotation survives that references a protocol type removed from the code, and no remaining annotation forces a wider record surface than the runtime provides.
rubrics.rationale: In this case the unification exists on two coupled surfaces (runtime records and ambient declarations); leaving either side referencing the other's now-removed shape breaks compilation of consumer code that the task forbids breaking.

rubrics.criterion: No scaffolding whose only purpose was to install or document the shared protocol is left behind: the kit functions, the capability-installation helper, or the interface block are deleted rather than left defined-and-unreferenced, in every emission format and in the declaration file.
rubrics.rationale: Both the kit functions and the shared interface in this case are pure unification scaffolding; keeping their definitions after removing their purposes would leave dead artifacts specific to this injection.

rubrics.criterion: The repair does not leave explanatory comments or doc-comment blocks advertising the one-uniform-surface design (a shared capability surface adopted by every helper's records) attached to members that now expose family-local surfaces.
rubrics.rationale: The injected kit, its interface, and one parameter doc comment narrate the cross-family unification; stale documentation of a removed design on surviving members is the documentation-shaped residue of this exact change.

rubrics.criterion: The repair does not break the promise-flavored families by leaving their call paths reading protocol members that no longer exist: consuming an async generator (including its return path), iterating with the async-values adapter, or applying a decorator must not raise a missing-member error (such as calling a capability that is no longer installed).
rubrics.rationale: Deleting or narrowing the shared kit without rewiring the three families that routed behavior through it (decorator validation, async-generator return wiring, async-value settlement) throws at construction or first use in this repository's runtime.

rubrics.criterion: The repair does not change the enumeration surface of any helper-produced record as user code observes it: the member sets visible through for-in, Object.keys, and Object.getOwnPropertyNames on returned generator records, iterator adapters, async adapters, and decorator contexts stay the same as before, and the disposal environments handed to the tracking helpers keep accepting the same fields.
rubrics.rationale: In this instance the protocol members were installed non-enumerably so user-visible enumeration stayed identical; a repair that installs family-local glue as enumerable members would change observable record state — the exact class of regression this case forbids.

rubrics.criterion: The repair does not narrow the declaration surface below what emitted code constructs: literal decorator-application context objects and literal disposal environments (the shapes compiler emit builds call sites with) remain assignable to the updated signatures, so no previously compiling call of the affected helpers stops compiling.
rubrics.rationale: The affected signatures belong to helpers whose arguments are generated by TS emit; the annotation change in this case made protocol members optional so literal emit shapes kept compiling, and any replacement annotation has to preserve that acceptance.
